title: PostgreSQL vs SQLite for a production application backend
meta_description: Compare PostgreSQL and SQLite for production backends across deployment, concurrent writes, operations, data types, and practical workload fit.
intro: PostgreSQL and SQLite both provide transactional SQL databases, but they place the database in different parts of the system. PostgreSQL runs as a separate server designed for networked, multi-user workloads. SQLite is an embedded library that reads and writes a local database file. That architectural difference should drive the choice.
verdict: Choose SQLite when one application instance owns the data, deployment simplicity matters, and write concurrency is modest. Choose PostgreSQL when several processes or services write concurrently, clients connect over a network, or the team needs server-side access control and broader operational tooling.

criteria.label: Operations
criteria.description: What must be deployed and maintained.

alternatives.name: PostgreSQL
alternatives.summary: A client-server relational database with network connections, server-managed concurrency, roles, extensions, and operational controls for multi-user applications.

specs.concurrency: Multiple concurrent readers and writers through MVCC
specs.operations: Server deployment, upgrades, backups and monitoring
specs.access: Native client connections over local or network transports
specs.fit: Shared production systems and write-heavy multi-user services

alternatives.name: SQLite
alternatives.summary: An embedded SQL database delivered as a library, with a portable single-file format and no separate database server to operate.

specs.architecture: Embedded library operating on a local file
specs.concurrency: Many readers; write transactions are serialized
specs.operations: No server process; application owns file lifecycle and backups
specs.access: In-process API rather than a built-in network service
specs.fit: Local application state, edge workloads, prototypes and read-heavy services

faq.question: Can SQLite run a real production application?
faq.answer: Yes. SQLite can be a strong production choice when the database is local to the application and the workload does not require many simultaneous writers or a built-in network database service.

faq.question: Does PostgreSQL automatically make an application more scalable?
faq.answer: No. PostgreSQL provides server-side concurrency and operational features, but application design, indexes, query patterns, connection management, and infrastructure still determine practical scale.

faq.question: When should a project migrate from SQLite to PostgreSQL?
faq.answer: Consider migration when write contention, multiple application instances, remote access, role-based controls, or database operations become persistent requirements rather than hypothetical future needs.

faq.question: Can both databases preserve transactional integrity?
faq.answer: Yes. Both support transactions and durability controls. Their concurrency models, deployment boundaries, and operational responsibilities differ, which changes how teams use those guarantees.
